niche.description:
Alexander Fleming found penicillin on a dish of germs in 1928, but he could only make a weak, impure liquid. It took Howard Florey, Ernst Chain and Norman Heatley at Oxford, and then American factories growing it in huge tanks, to make enough to treat people. By D-Day there was enough for the wounded.

niche.title: How Penicillin's Accidental Discovery Saved Millions of Lives
niche.description: What if a tiny patch of mold changed medicine forever? Discover the incredible true story of penicillin, one of the most important medical breakthroughs in history. In 1928, Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming noticed that mold growing on a laboratory culture was preventing nearby bacteria from growing. This unexpected observation opened the door to a discovery that would eventually transform the treatment of bacterial infections. Learn about the challenges faced in extracting penicillin, the Oxford scientists who developed it, and how it became essential during World War II.

niche.title: The Messy Lab That Saved Millions 🦠
niche.description:
The mistake that saved millions of lives! 🧬
In 1928, Alexander Fleming left his messy lab for a two-week vacation. When he returned, a forgotten petri dish was covered in mold—and a mysterious clear ring proved the mold was killing the surrounding bacteria. That accidental discovery became penicillin, changing modern medicine forever.
Would a tidier scientist have washed the dish? Let us know in the comments! 👇

niche.title: His Messy Lab Gave Us Penicillin
niche.description: London, summer 1928. Alexander Fleming, a bacteriologist at St Mary's Hospital, left a pile of staph culture dishes on his bench and went on holiday. In September he found one had grown a mould, and around it the bacteria had disappeared. He called the substance penicillin, but he couldn't purify it or make enough to use as a medicine, and his 1929 paper drew almost no attention. Almost ten years later, Howard Florey and Ernst Chain in Oxford picked it up again. In May 1940 they infected eight mice and treated four: by morning only the treated four were alive. niche.title: Penicillin: The Market Melon That Helped Save Lives | WW2 Oddities #8
niche.description:
Part 8 of WW2 Oddities.

In 1943, scientists in Peoria, Illinois, found a high-producing penicillin mold on a rotten cantaloupe from a local market. That strain and its improved descendants helped scale up penicillin production, with millions of doses ready for Allied troops by D-Day in 1944.

niche.title: What if Antibiotics Stopped Working? Part 1
niche.description:
Part 1 of 3. In 1924, 16-year-old Calvin Coolidge Jr., the U.S. president's son, got a blister on his toe playing tennis at the White House. It became infected, and he died of blood poisoning on July 7. Penicillin was discovered four years later, though it took more than another decade to become a usable medicine. Today, some bacteria are evolving resistance to the drugs we rely on.

outliers.title: His Dirty Dishes Saved MILLIONS
outliers.description:
How was penicillin discovered? Alexander Fleming went on holiday in 1928 and left his dirty lab dishes out. When he came back, mould had killed the germs around it.

Fleming worked at St Mary’s Hospital in London. In September 1928 he found that a blue-green mould on one of his dishes had cleared a ring of dead bacteria around itself. He named the substance penicillin. It took a team in Oxford, led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain, until about 1940 to turn it into a medicine, and they grew the mould in bedpans and milk churns.
